name: Bulgarian state trunk: Първо Българско царство → Vtoro Balgarsko Tsarstvo → Ottoman → Bulgaria
description: Bulgarian state-formation: from the First Bulgarian Empire (681-1018, founded by Khan Asparuh), through Byzantine reconquest (1018-1185), Second Bulgarian Empire (1185-1396), Ottoman rule (~500 years), and the modern Bulgarian state from 1878. The chain shows two distinct 'imperial' periods followed by a long gap under foreign rule.
ethical_notes: The Bulgarian 'Yoke' (1396-1878) narrative is politically loaded: Ottoman rule was oppressive in periods (especially the 19th century decline) but Bulgarian identity persisted through the Orthodox Church. The Second Bulgarian Empire's fall at Velbazhd (1330) and Nicopolis (1396) are often nationalist anchors, but the Ottoman period saw genuine cultural persistence (the Tarnovo literary school, Damascene preachers, the National Revival from ~1760).

sources.citation: Crampton, R. J. 'A Concise History of Bulgaria' (2005)
Fine, J. V. A. 'The Early Medieval Balkans' (1983) and 'The Late Medieval Balkans' (1987)

links.description: First Bulgarian Empire (681-1018), founded by Khan Asparuh after the Byzantine-Bulgar Treaty of 681. Christianized under Boris I (864); developed the Cyrillic script under Clement of Ohrid (late 9th c.). Conquered by Byzantine Emperor Basil II 'the Bulgar-slayer' at Kleidion (1014) and fully absorbed by 1018.

Second Bulgarian Empire founded by the Asen brothers (Ivan Asen I and Peter) in 1185 after a Byzantine tax revolt. Peaked under Ivan Asen II (1218-1241), then fragmented. Fell piece by piece to the Ottomans (Tarnovo 1393, Vidin 1396).
Bulgaria fully incorporated into the Ottoman Empire after the fall of the Tsardom of Vidin (1396). No Bulgarian state existed for ~500 years.
links.ethical_notes: The devshirme (child levy) and millet system shaped Bulgarian experience under Ottoman rule. The 19th-century April Uprising (1876) was brutally suppressed (Batak massacre), triggering Russian intervention.

name: Serbian state trunk: Raska → Srpsko Carstvo → Српска деспотовина → Ottoman → Кнежевина Србија → Југославија (СХС → СФРЈ → СРЈ → СЦГ) → Република Србија
description: Serbian state-formation: from the medieval Grand Principality of Rascia (Raška), through the zenith of the Serbian Empire under Stefan Dušan (1346-1371), the fragmenting Serbian Despotate (1402-1459), the long Ottoman period, and eventual revival from 1804 (First Serbian Uprising). Ottoman-era Serbian identity persisted through the Orthodox Patriarchate of Peć (restored 1557).
ethical_notes: Serbian national historiography centers the Battle of Kosovo (1389) as the defining tragedy; more recent scholarship notes Serbian nobles fought on BOTH sides at Kosovo, and the battle was not immediately decisive. The Yugoslav period (1918-2006) is contested — Serb-centric vs federal readings diverge. The 1990s Yugoslav Wars are recent enough that historiographic consensus is still forming.

sources.citation: Fine, J. V. A. 'The Late Medieval Balkans' (1987)
Ramet, S. P. 'The Three Yugoslavias: State-Building and Legitimation, 1918-2005' (2006)

links.description: Grand Principality of Rascia (Raška), the medieval Serbian state under the Nemanjić dynasty from c. 1083. Stefan Nemanja (r. 1166-1196) and his son Stefan the First-Crowned established the state's independence from Byzantium.

Serbian Empire under Stefan Uroš IV Dušan, crowned 'Emperor of Serbs and Greeks' at Skopje on 16 April 1346. Controlled most of the Balkans. Collapsed after Dušan's death (1355) — a classic case of over-extension.

Serbian Despotate (1402-1459), a diminished Serbian state formed after the Battle of Ankara weakened Ottoman pressure. Stefan Lazarević and George Branković ruled as Ottoman vassals. Fell to the Ottomans at Smederevo (20 June 1459).
Serbia fully incorporated into the Ottoman Empire. The Patriarchate of Peć (restored 1557) became the vehicle of Serbian religious and cultural identity through 400 years of Ottoman rule.
links.ethical_notes: The Great Migrations of Serbs (1690, 1739) into Habsburg territory reshaped the ethnic map of the Balkans and are often cited in modern Serbian-Croatian disputes.

links.description: Serbian self-rule re-emerged from the Ottoman Empire through the uprisings of 1804-1815: de facto autonomy from the Second Uprising settlement (1815), hereditary autonomous principality by hatt-i sharif (1830), full international independence at the Treaty of Berlin (1878), kingdom from 1882.
links.ethical_notes: The transition was a violent decolonization (two uprisings, 1804-13 and 1815). ETHICS-002: the consolidating Serbian state was also a perpetrator - the 1862-67 removal of the Muslim population from the garrison towns and the 1878 expulsions from the Nis/Toplica sanjaks (~49,000 Albanians among at least 71,000 Muslims) are recorded on the entity.

links.description: On 1 December 1918 the Kingdom of Serbia merged with the State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs (and, via the contested Podgorica Assembly, with Montenegro) into the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, renamed Yugoslavia in 1929.
links.ethical_notes: The Serbia-side unification was negotiated and peaceful; the Montenegrin absorption was contested and its aftermath violent (Christmas Uprising 1919) - see the Montenegrin chain, where that link is typed ANNEXATION.

links.description: The Axis invasion (April 1941) destroyed the kingdom; after four years of occupation, partition, genocide (NDH camps, Jasenovac) and multi-sided war, the communist Partisans established the Federal People's Republic (AVNOJ 1943; monarchy abolished 29 November 1945).
links.ethical_notes: The 1941-45 period saw occupation, the Holocaust and the Ustasa genocide of Serbs, Roma and Jews, and civil war among resistance movements - the socialist state emerged from that violence, not from a peaceful succession.

links.description: As the SFR Yugoslavia broke up in the 1991-1995 wars (Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia, Macedonia seceding), Serbia and Montenegro proclaimed the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on 27 April 1992 as the rump/claimed-continuator state.
links.ethical_notes: is_violent=true: the FRY was born from the violent dissolution of the SFRY (Yugoslav wars, including the Srebrenica genocide of 1995 by Bosnian Serb forces, and the 1998-99 Kosovo war and NATO intervention involving FRY forces). Milošević-era Serbia was a principal party; perpetrator roles are named on the relevant entities.

links.entity_name: Државна заједница Србија и Црна Гора
links.description: The Constitutional Charter of 4 February 2003 restructured the FRY into the loose State Union of Serbia and Montenegro, retiring the name 'Yugoslavia' after 74 years (EU-mediated, the 'Solania' arrangement).
links.ethical_notes: A constitutional restructuring/renaming, not a violent transition. Kosovo remained de iure part of Serbia but under UN administration (UNMIK, UNSC Res 1244).

links.description: Montenegro's independence referendum of 21 May 2006 (55.5% vs the EU-set 55% threshold) led to Montenegro's declaration of independence on 3 June 2006; Serbia's National Assembly declared the Republic of Serbia the successor state on 5 June 2006.
links.ethical_notes: Peaceful secession by referendum. Both historiographies on the 55% threshold and the union are recorded on the Serbia-and-Montenegro entity; the unresolved Kosovo dispute (2008 UDI) is recorded on the Republic of Serbia entity, not arbitrated.

name: Romanian principalities → Kingdom → Republic
description: Romanian state-formation: the medieval principalities of Wallachia (Țara Românească, c. 1330) and Moldavia (1346), both Ottoman vassals, united under Alexandru Ioan Cuza (1859), independent 1878, proclaimed the Kingdom of Romania under Carol I (1881-1947).
ethical_notes: Transylvania's integration (1918) changed the ethnic balance and is still contested by Hungarian historiography. The interwar 'Greater Romania' included significant Ukrainian (Bessarabia) and Hungarian (Transylvania) minorities. Romania's alignment with Nazi Germany (1940-1944) and the Iași pogroms are significant; Ceaușescu's nationalist narrative minimized them. NOTE (ETHICS-001): the early-Wallachia entity 'Furstentum Walachei' (a German-language name) was removed from this chain in favor of the local-named Țara Românească; that entity's German name_original is itself slated for an entity-level rename/deprecation.

sources.citation: Hitchins, K. 'A Concise History of Romania' (2014)
Castellan, G. 'A History of the Romanians' (1989)

links.description: Principality of Wallachia (Țara Românească), founded by Basarab I c. 1330 after independence from the Kingdom of Hungary at the Battle of Posada (1330). It produced Vlad III Țepeș (the historical basis for Dracula). An Ottoman vassal from the 16th century while retaining internal autonomy.

Principality of Moldavia, founded 1346 under Dragoș as a Hungarian march, achieving independence under Bogdan I (1359). Stephen the Great (1457-1504) resisted Ottoman expansion. Wallachia and Moldavia were PARALLEL principalities (not one succeeding the other), both Ottoman vassals from the 16th century; the linear order here is a model artifact — they unite at the next node.

United Principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia, formed when Alexandru Ioan Cuza was elected prince of both Moldavia (Jan 1859) and Wallachia (Feb 1859); formal union as Romania in 1862, full independence in 1878 (Treaty of Berlin, after the violent 1877-78 Russo-Turkish war). Proclaimed the Kingdom of Romania (Regatul României) under Carol I in 1881; the monarchy lasted until 1947, when it was abolished under Soviet pressure.
links.ethical_notes: Greater Romania (1918) integrated Transylvania, Bessarabia, and Bukovina, changing the ethnic balance — still contested by Hungarian historiography. Romania's alignment with Nazi Germany (1940-44) and the Iași pogrom (1941, ~13,000 Jews killed) are part of the record; Ceaușescu's nationalist narrative minimized them.
